questions.question: What does IDP stand for in the context of Platform Engineering?
questions.explanation: IDP stands for Internal Developer Platform — a self-service layer for development teams.
options: Internet Data Protocol
Internal Developer Platform
Integrated Deployment Pipeline
Infrastructure Design Pattern

questions.question: What are "golden paths" in platform engineering?
questions.explanation: Golden paths are pre-configured workflows that encode best practices while still allowing flexibility.
options: Physical pathways in the office
Pre-configured, opinionated workflows that encode best practices
Premium-tier cloud service plans
Network routing protocols

questions.question: What key principle does a platform team follow regarding development teams?
questions.explanation: The platform reduces cognitive load on development teams so they can focus on business logic rather than infrastructure plumbing.
options: All code must be reviewed by the platform team
Development teams should never touch infrastructure
Reduce cognitive load so teams focus on business logic
Every team must use the same programming language

questions.question: Instead of every team building their own CI/CD pipelines, what does a platform team provide?
questions.explanation: Platform teams create golden paths — reusable, pre-configured workflows — so individual teams don't reinvent the wheel.
options: A mandate that no CI/CD is needed
Pre-configured, reusable golden path workflows
A single monolithic deployment pipeline for all teams
Outsourced DevOps consulting

questions.question: What is the combined philosophy behind platform engineering?
questions.explanation: Platform engineering combines ownership ("you build it, you run it") with support ("we make running it easy").
options: "Move fast and break things"
"You build it, you run it" combined with "We make running it easy"
"Don't repeat yourself" and "Keep it simple"
"Fail fast" and "Ship often"

questions.question: What is an anti-pattern in platform engineering?
questions.explanation: Forcing teams to use a platform that doesn't provide clear value is a common anti-pattern that breeds resentment.
options: Making the platform optional
Starting with a small platform
Mandating platform use without providing value
Measuring developer satisfaction

questions.question: According to Team Topologies, what is a Platform Team's primary interaction mode?
questions.explanation: Platform Teams provide capabilities via "X-as-a-Service" — teams consume with minimal coordination.
options: Collaboration
Facilitation
X-as-a-Service
Pair programming

questions.question: What is the "Thinnest Viable Platform" (TVP) concept?
questions.explanation: TVP means starting small — even a wiki page with best practices — and evolving toward self-service APIs as needs grow.
options: Using the cheapest possible cloud provider
Starting with the smallest platform that provides value, possibly just documentation
Removing all features except deployment
Running on the minimum number of servers

questions.question: Which of these is a key metric for platform success according to the deep dive?
questions.explanation: Key metrics include onboarding time, time to first deploy, change failure rate, and developer satisfaction surveys.
options: Lines of code written per day
Number of microservices deployed
Developer onboarding time and developer satisfaction
Total number of cloud resources provisioned

questions.question: Which book is a primary theoretical foundation of Platform Engineering?
questions.explanation: Team Topologies by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais defines four team types, including the Platform team and its X-as-a-Service interaction mode.
options: "Clean Code" by Robert C. Martin
"Team Topologies" by Skelton and Pais
"The Phoenix Project" by Gene Kim
"Accelerate" by Nicole Forsgren

questions.question: How many fundamental team types does Team Topologies identify?
questions.explanation: Team Topologies defines four team types: Stream-aligned, Enabling, Complicated Subsystem, and Platform.
options: Two
Three
Four
Six

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four team types in Team Topologies?
questions.explanation: "Architecture team" is not one of the four Team Topologies types. The four are: Stream-aligned, Enabling, Complicated Subsystem, and Platform.
options: Stream-aligned
Enabling
Architecture
Complicated Subsystem

questions.question: What does a Platform team provide to enable "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: The platform makes "running it easy" so product teams can own their services without being overwhelmed by infrastructure complexity.
options: A separate operations team to handle production incidents
A self-service platform that reduces the cognitive load of owning services
Code reviews for every production deployment
Mandatory training on cloud infrastructure

questions.question: Without golden paths, what problem does each development team face?
questions.explanation: Without golden paths, every team reinvents the same infrastructure — creating inconsistency and wasting effort on undifferentiated work.
options: They cannot write tests
Every team must reinvent CI/CD, monitoring, and infrastructure from scratch
Teams cannot deploy independently
Teams must use the same programming language

questions.question: What does "self-service" mean in the context of an Internal Developer Platform?
questions.explanation: Self-service means teams access platform capabilities on demand — no tickets, no waiting for a human in the platform team to act.
options: Teams write all their own tools
Teams can provision infrastructure and run workflows without waiting for the platform team
Developers interview and hire themselves
Teams manage their own payroll systems

questions.question: What is the primary goal of reducing cognitive load on development teams?
questions.explanation: Cognitive load reduction means developers can focus on the unique value they create — the business problem — rather than infrastructure boilerplate.
options: To make developers work fewer hours
To let teams focus on business logic and product delivery instead of infrastructure plumbing
To reduce the number of engineers needed
To simplify the codebase

questions.question: A developer needs a new database environment for testing. In an ideal Platform Engineering setup, they should:
questions.explanation: X-as-a-Service means stream-aligned teams consume platform capabilities on demand — self-service with minimal coordination.
options: Open a ticket and wait for the platform team to provision it
Provision it themselves via a self-service API with no coordination needed
Ask their manager to escalate to ops
Use their local laptop instead

questions.question: Which scenario is an example of the "mandating platform use without providing value" anti-pattern?
questions.explanation: Forcing adoption of a platform that slows teams down breeds resentment and resistance — the opposite of what Platform Engineering aims for.
options: Requiring teams to use a platform that halves their deployment time
Forcing teams to use a slow, unreliable CI/CD system with no alternative
Providing a golden path that most teams adopt voluntarily
Offering optional platform tooling with good documentation

questions.question: What is the key reason a Platform team should treat its platform as a "product"?
questions.explanation: Treating the platform as a product means understanding developer needs, gathering feedback, and iterating — just like any customer-facing product.
options: It generates direct revenue for the company
It has internal customers whose feedback should shape its features and evolution
Products have better tooling than platforms
It helps justify the platform team's headcount

questions.question: Why is measuring "developer onboarding time" a useful platform metric?
questions.explanation: Onboarding time reflects the platform's ability to make new engineers productive quickly — a direct signal of self-service quality.
options: It measures the quality of the HR hiring process
It reveals whether the platform truly makes it easy for new engineers to become productive quickly
It tracks how fast developers learn to program
It measures documentation quality in isolation

questions.question: A stream-aligned team wants to use a technology not covered by any golden path. What should the platform team's response be?
questions.explanation: Golden paths provide defaults and best practices but are not prisons — allowing flexibility while encoding opinions is core to the design.
options: Refuse — all teams must use golden paths strictly
Mandate they adopt an existing path regardless of fit
Golden paths are opinionated but flexible; support the team in making an appropriate choice
Transfer the team to a different business unit

questions.question: What distinguishes a Platform team's interaction mode from an Enabling team's?
questions.explanation: X-as-a-Service means minimum coordination; facilitation means active collaboration to raise capability. These are distinct interaction modes in Team Topologies.
options: Platform teams pair-program with stream-aligned teams; Enabling teams don't
Platform teams provide X-as-a-Service (minimal coordination); Enabling teams facilitate and upskill (temporary collaboration)
Enabling teams are always larger than Platform teams
Platform teams are owned by IT; Enabling teams by engineering

questions.question: What does "building too much too early" risk in a Platform Engineering context?
questions.explanation: The Thinnest Viable Platform principle guards against this: start with what provides value now and evolve based on actual demand.
options: Building a platform that is too fast to use
Overinvesting in features nobody needs yet, delaying value delivery and creating a maintenance burden
Creating security vulnerabilities
Hiring too many platform engineers

questions.question: The four team types in Team Topologies, in full, are:
questions.explanation: Team Topologies identifies exactly four types: Stream-aligned (delivery), Enabling (upskilling), Complicated Subsystem (specialist knowledge), and Platform (X-as-a-Service).
options: Product, Dev, Ops, QA
Frontend, Backend, Infrastructure, Security
Stream-aligned, Enabling, Complicated Subsystem, Platform
Feature, Support, Architecture, Operations

questions.question: According to the deep dive, which signal most directly indicates that developers actually value the platform?
questions.explanation: A good platform is one developers voluntarily choose — forced adoption masks whether the platform actually helps.
options: The number of golden paths defined
The size of the platform engineering team
Voluntary adoption — developers choose to use it without being mandated
The number of cloud resources the platform manages

questions.question: The deep dive identifies "treating the platform as a pure infrastructure concern" as an anti-pattern. What should it be treated as instead?
questions.explanation: A platform that ignores its users' experience fails. Treating it as a product means continuous discovery of developer needs and iterating on the offering.
options: A security system
A cost center
A product with internal customers
A compliance tool

questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly cited as a key platform success metric in the deep dive?
questions.explanation: Time to first deploy — how quickly a new team can ship to production — is a direct indicator of how well the platform reduces friction.
options: Cost per cloud resource
Number of microservices deployed
Time to first deploy
Lines of platform code written

questions.question: What distinguishes the "Complicated Subsystem" team type from a Platform team?
questions.explanation: Complicated Subsystem teams exist for genuinely complex technical domains requiring deep expertise (e.g. video encoding). Platform teams provide broad, reusable capabilities as a service.
options: Complicated Subsystem teams provide infrastructure; Platform teams provide expertise
Complicated Subsystem teams own deep specialist knowledge for a complex domain; Platform teams provide broad self-service capabilities
Platform teams are always larger
Complicated Subsystem teams use X-as-a-Service

questions.question: The "Thinnest Viable Platform" can start as just a wiki page. What principle does this reflect?
questions.explanation: TVP is a lean approach: deliver value immediately with minimal investment, then add self-service APIs, portals, and automation as actual needs emerge.
options: Documentation is always more important than code
Platform Engineering doesn't require any tooling
Start with the minimum that provides real value and evolve incrementally based on proven demand
Wikis are the best developer tooling available

questions.question: According to Team Topologies, what is the "cognitive load" problem that Platform teams are specifically designed to solve for stream-aligned teams?
questions.explanation: Stream-aligned teams focus on delivering value; offloading infrastructure complexity to a Platform team keeps that cognitive load within manageable bounds.
options: Too many programming languages to learn
The burden of managing infrastructure, tooling, and operational complexity on top of delivering product features
Too many meetings with stakeholders
Having too many microservices to maintain

questions.question: Which statement best describes vertical scaling ("scale up")?
questions.explanation: Scaling up means replacing the existing machine with a larger one. There is still only one node.
options: Adding more identical servers behind a load balancer
Making a single server bigger — more CPU, more RAM, faster disks
Splitting the database into many shards
Moving the workload to a different data centre

questions.question: Which statement best describes horizontal scaling ("scale out")?
questions.explanation: Scaling out means adding more nodes so the workload can be spread across them.
options: Upgrading the CPU to a higher clock speed
Running more copies of the service behind a load balancer
Rewriting the application in a faster language
Moving from spinning disks to SSDs

questions.question: A key reliability advantage of horizontal scaling over vertical scaling is…
questions.explanation: A fleet of N nodes behind a load balancer tolerates single-node failure; one big box does not.
options: Lower software-licence cost per core
No single point of failure — one node can die and the service stays up
Guaranteed strong consistency without any extra work
Faster CPU per request

questions.question: Which kind of workload is the easiest to scale horizontally?
questions.explanation: Stateless services can run as N identical copies — any request can land on any node.
options: A stateful legacy monolith that holds sessions in memory
A stateless HTTP service behind a load balancer
A single-writer SQL database
A desktop application

questions.question: Why do teams often reach for vertical scaling first on a classic SQL database?
questions.explanation: Keeping everything on one node sidesteps the hard problems of replication and partitioning, at least for a while.
options: It is always cheaper at every scale
A single node preserves a single source of truth — no need to redesign for distribution
Vertical scaling automatically turns the database into a NoSQL store
It removes the need for backups

questions.question: Which pattern extends horizontal scaling to stateful systems by partitioning data by key?
questions.explanation: Sharding partitions data (by user id, tenant, range, etc.) so each shard fits on a node that can still be scaled up.
options: Caching
Sharding
Blue-green deployment
Feature flagging

questions.question: Which of these is a real limitation of vertical scaling?
questions.explanation: The top instance SKUs are disproportionately expensive and eventually run out — physics and vendor price lists both impose ceilings.
options: There is always a hard ceiling — even the biggest instance has a top size, and cost rises non-linearly near it
Vertical scaling prevents the use of containers
Scaling up requires rewriting the application in a new language
Vertical scaling makes horizontal scaling impossible later

questions.question: Which trade-off is introduced specifically by scaling a stateful system horizontally (vs keeping it vertical)?
questions.explanation: A distributed stateful system must pick, during a partition, between rejecting writes (CP) or serving stale data (AP). A single node sidesteps the question.
options: The CAP trade-off between Consistency and Availability during network partitions
The need to compile code to native binaries
A requirement to use a proprietary operating system
The loss of all ACID guarantees in every case

questions.question: Horizontal scaling pairs naturally with which operational technique for elastic capacity?
questions.explanation: Adding/removing nodes is what autoscalers (Kubernetes HPA, AWS ASG, serverless concurrency) do in response to live load signals.
options: Scheduled downtime windows for weekly resizing
Autoscaling driven by signals such as CPU, queue depth, or p95 latency
Manual re-provisioning per release
Fixing the fleet size permanently at its peak demand

questions.question: Who coined the phrase "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: Werner Vogels coined the phrase in a 2006 ACM Queue interview to describe how AWS teams work.
options: Martin Fowler
Werner Vogels (Amazon CTO)
Kent Beck
Gene Kim

questions.question: In "you build it, you run it," who carries the pager when a service breaks in production?
questions.explanation: The team that built the service also operates it — closing the feedback loop between design and production behaviour.
options: A separate 24/7 operations team
The developers who wrote the service
The security team
The CTO

questions.question: Which model does "you build it, you run it" replace?
questions.explanation: It replaces the old relay race where developers handed finished code to a separate ops team that hadn't designed it.
options: Agile sprints
Test-driven development
The "throw code over the wall" handoff between dev and ops
Pair programming

questions.question: Why does being on-call for your own service tend to improve its design?
questions.explanation: The pager is a direct feedback signal: pain felt by the author becomes reliability improvements in the next release.
options: It forces developers to work longer hours
On-call hours count toward performance reviews
When you personally get paged at 3 a.m., you invest in reliability and fix root causes
On-call rotations generate more commits

questions.question: Which advantage for a dev team does "you build it, you run it" NOT directly provide?
questions.explanation: Ownership is end-to-end, but teams still collaborate — typically with a Platform team that makes "running it" easy.
options: Faster feedback from production
Tighter ownership and autonomy
A guarantee that the team never needs other teams
Growth of SRE / deployment skills across the team

questions.question: Which real-world analogy best captures "you build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: The chef hears complaints in real time and iterates the menu — a tight feedback loop the factory-canteen model lacks.
options: A novelist who hires a ghostwriter
A restaurant chef who also works the dining room and hears customers directly
A courier who only delivers pre-packaged boxes
A librarian organizing other people's books

questions.question: Which research programme links end-to-end team ownership to the "four key metrics" (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, MTTR)?
questions.explanation: DORA's Accelerate research shows teams practicing "you build it, you run it" consistently outperform on all four key delivery metrics.
options: ISO 9001
DORA / State of DevOps (Accelerate)
ITIL
CMMI

questions.question: What is the main risk of adopting "you build it, you run it" without a supporting Platform team?
questions.explanation: Without a "thinnest viable platform" to reduce cognitive load, full ownership can crush product teams — Team Topologies pairs the two patterns deliberately.
options: Developers become too specialized in one area
Cognitive overload — every team must also master Kubernetes, tracing and incident response
Code reviews become mandatory
Services are deployed too infrequently

questions.question: Which complementary practice is NOT typically listed alongside "you build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: Quarterly change-board releases are the opposite pattern — they recreate the dev/ops wall the principle is designed to remove.
options: Blameless post-mortems and error budgets
Feature flags and progressive (canary / blue-green) deployment
Production-grade observability built in from day one
Quarterly "big bang" release windows managed by a change board

questions.question: In what year did Werner Vogels describe "You build it, you run it" in ACM Queue?
questions.explanation: Werner Vogels described the approach in a 2006 ACM Queue interview about how AWS teams operate.

questions.question: "You build it, you run it" is primarily about closing which gap?
questions.explanation: The principle closes the loop between writing software and operating it in production — making developers feel the consequences of their own decisions.
options: The gap between frontend and backend teams
The gap between developers and the operational reality of their software
The gap between senior and junior engineers
The gap between engineering and HR

questions.question: Which of these is part of "end-to-end ownership" in "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: End-to-end ownership means the team is responsible for the full lifecycle — from design through to post-incident reviews.
options: Only writing and testing the code
Only deploying the code to staging
Design, code, CI/CD, deployment, observability, on-call, and post-incident learning
Writing code and handing it to a separate ops team

questions.question: What was the key problem with the old "relay race" development model?
questions.explanation: In the relay race, responsibility was split: devs wrote code they didn't run; ops ran code they didn't write. Incidents dragged because understanding and accountability were separated.
options: It was too fast for organizations to manage
Developers handed code to ops who hadn't designed it — ops couldn't diagnose problems; developers didn't feel the pain
Ops teams were less skilled than developers
It required too many project managers

questions.question: How does "You build it, you run it" improve the quality of technical design?
questions.explanation: On-call is a powerful design signal: pain caused by your own code motivates you to fix root causes and build reliability in from the start.
options: By requiring more code reviews
By giving developers financial incentives for reliability
When you get paged for your own service's failures, you stop shipping code that causes them
By assigning dedicated QA engineers to each team

questions.question: What skills do developers gain through "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: End-to-end ownership exposes developers to the full operational landscape, growing skills in deployment, observability, and incident response.
options: Primarily UI/UX design skills
Deployment, monitoring, and SRE skills that make them stronger engineers
Marketing and sales skills
Project management certifications

questions.question: What does "clear ownership" mean in the context of "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: Clear ownership means one team is accountable end-to-end — for how the service performs in production, not just whether the code compiles.
options: One developer owns all the code
One team is accountable for outcomes, not just outputs
One manager signs off on all changes
One repository per team

questions.question: A team is on-call for their own service and notices the same alert fires every Monday morning. What should they do under "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: The on-call rotation is a feedback signal. The team that owns the service is in the best position — and has the strongest motivation — to fix root causes, not just escalate.
options: Accept it as normal maintenance overhead
Escalate to the ops team for investigation
Fix the root cause — they have both the authority and the motivation to do so
Mute the alert until the next quarter's prioritization

questions.question: What does "autonomy" specifically mean for a team practicing "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: Autonomy means the team controls its own destiny: no waiting for ops approvals, no handoff queues — the same people who build can deploy and iterate.
options: The team works without any coordination with other teams
No tickets to another team, no handoff delays — the team controls its own deployment decisions
The team has no technical standards to follow
Developers choose their own compensation

questions.question: Why does "You build it, you run it" lead to "pride of craftsmanship"?
questions.explanation: Owning outcomes means the team sees the full picture including failures. That accountability and visibility restores pride in the quality of the work.
options: Because teams are evaluated on code quality metrics
Because when you own outcomes end-to-end — not just outputs — you care whether the service actually works well in production
Because managers reward quality more under this model
Because the team presents their work to the CEO

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates why "You build it, you run it" breaks down WITHOUT platform support?
questions.explanation: Without a platform to absorb infrastructure complexity, full ownership becomes cognitive overload — defeating the purpose of the principle.
options: A team deploys to staging without running tests
A team must also master Kubernetes, distributed tracing, and incident response simultaneously — leaving no capacity for product work
A team ships features too infrequently
A team has no QA engineer

questions.question: How does "You build it, you run it" change the relationship between code quality and developer incentives?
questions.explanation: Unlike the relay-race model where devs never feel production pain, YBYR makes poor reliability personally painful for its authors — aligning incentives powerfully.
options: Code quality becomes a management concern only
Developers are paid more for reliable code
Poor reliability means worse on-call for the authors, so reliability becomes a first-class design goal from the start
Quality gates are enforced entirely by the build system

questions.question: What does "pager fatigue" refer to, and why is it a risk under "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: Pager fatigue occurs when on-call becomes a constant burden — poor alert hygiene, no follow-the-sun rotation, and insufficient tooling turn ownership into punishment.
options: Fatigue from carrying heavy physical pagers
Burnout caused by excessive on-call alerts without good tooling or rotation — unsustainable over time
Alert desensitization from too many monitoring dashboards
Developers refusing to participate in on-call at all

questions.question: The info content says YBYR is "less a process than a feedback loop." What does this mean?
questions.explanation: The insight is that YBYR's value is systemic: every architectural decision receives an operational signal, and that continuous feedback transforms how teams think and design.
options: It cannot be documented or standardized
The value isn't in the process steps but in the continuous signal flowing from operational reality back to design decisions
Feedback loops require automated testing only
It means retrospectives are more important than releases

questions.question: Which of the four DORA metrics specifically measures the time from code commit to running in production?
questions.explanation: Lead time for changes measures the elapsed time between committing code and that code running in production — a key indicator of delivery efficiency.
options: Deployment frequency
Lead time for changes
Change failure rate
Mean Time to Restore (MTTR)

questions.question: The deep dive describes "unclear boundaries" as a failure mode. Why does a shared monolith with no ownership lines cause this?
questions.explanation: YBYR requires clear service boundaries. Without them, ownership is diffuse — the on-call question "who's responsible?" has no answer, and incidents drag on.
options: Monoliths are inherently unreliable
No team has a clear boundary, so production problems become "no-one's problem" — everyone is accountable, so no-one is
Monoliths cannot be deployed independently
Shared code always has slower test suites

questions.question: According to the deep dive, how is a well-run on-call rotation different from a punishment?
questions.explanation: On-call is a feedback mechanism: each page is information about a design flaw the team is uniquely positioned to fix. Handled well, it continuously improves the system.
options: Well-run on-call pays more per alert
It is the signal that drives design improvement — repeated alerts give the team both the motivation and authority to fix root causes
It involves fewer alerts by design
It runs only during business hours

questions.question: The deep dive lists "feature flags" as a complementary practice. What specific risk do feature flags help manage?
questions.explanation: Feature flags decouple deployment from release — code goes to production (fast feedback) while only being exposed to a subset of users, limiting risk.
options: They reduce the total number of features shipped
They allow teams to release code to production while controlling exposure — reducing blast radius if something goes wrong
They replace automated testing
They prevent the need for rollbacks entirely

questions.question: The deep dive says YBYR is the "cultural foundation of DevOps." What does "cultural foundation" mean here?
questions.explanation: YBYR is not a practice or tool — it's the cultural shift that makes DevOps practices meaningful. Without the ownership mindset, tools alone don't deliver the benefits.
options: DevOps is a culture created by Werner Vogels
YBYR embodies the values and mindset that DevOps practices are built on — ownership, feedback, and shared accountability between build and run
YBYR requires a specific DevOps toolchain to work
DevOps culture is defined by DORA metrics alone

questions.question: The deep dive says YBYR turns a developer into a "systems thinker." What specific capability does this describe?
questions.explanation: A systems thinker understands the full feedback loop: design choices become operational realities, and operational pain is a signal about design flaws.
options: Thinking only about distributed systems patterns
Understanding that every architectural decision has operational consequences, and designing with both in mind
Learning Kubernetes and observability tools
Managing a team as well as writing code

questions.question: Progressive deployment (canary / blue-green) is listed as complementary to YBYR. What specific problem does it solve?
questions.explanation: Progressive deployment reduces risk by limiting blast radius: a canary rollout exposes a small percentage of traffic to the new version before full release.
options: It automates documentation updates after deployment
It reduces cloud costs through resource sharing
It allows teams to validate changes in production incrementally before full rollout — reducing change failure rate
It replaces the need for a staging environment entirely

questions.question: What does a Web Application Firewall (WAF) primarily inspect?
questions.explanation: A WAF operates at layer 7 — it inspects HTTP(S) traffic and blocks requests that match attack patterns before they reach the application.
options: Disk I/O on the application server
HTTP(S) requests and responses to the application
Outbound DNS lookups from the datacentre
SSH sessions to production hosts

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic attack a WAF is designed to stop?
questions.explanation: WAFs specialise in application-layer attacks such as SQL injection, XSS, path traversal and command injection — the OWASP Top 10 territory.
options: A phishing email sent to an employee
SQL injection in a login form
A stolen laptop in an airport
A misconfigured backup job

questions.question: Where is a WAF typically deployed?
questions.explanation: A WAF sits at the edge so one rule set protects every service behind it, including legacy apps that cannot easily be changed.
options: Inside the database engine
On every developer laptop
In front of the application — at the CDN, load balancer or ingress
As a client-side JavaScript library

questions.question: What is a "false positive" in WAF terms?
questions.explanation: A false positive is a legitimate request wrongly flagged as malicious. False negatives are the opposite — real attacks that slip through.
options: An attack the WAF failed to detect
A legitimate request that the WAF incorrectly blocks
A rule that has been disabled
A successful deployment of a new rule

questions.question: Why are false positives particularly painful for a product team?
questions.explanation: False positives present to users as cryptic 403s and to the team as "the app is broken" tickets — the cost is visible on the product side, not the security side.
options: They make the security dashboard look too green
They silently break real user journeys and generate support tickets that look like application bugs
They reduce CPU utilisation on the WAF
They force a rollback of the application version

questions.question: What is the recommended way to roll out a new WAF rule in production?
questions.explanation: Detect-only first lets you see which legitimate traffic the rule would have blocked. Skipping this step is the most common way a WAF takes down its own application.
options: Enable it in prevent mode immediately so no attacks slip through
Deploy it only on weekends
Start in detect-only (log) mode, observe a full traffic cycle, then switch to prevent mode
Apply it exclusively to authenticated users first

questions.question: Why is tuning a WAF a collaboration between the platform team and the product team?
questions.explanation: The platform team owns the WAF capability; the product team owns the knowledge of normal traffic. Good rules are a joint product of both.
options: Because the platform team needs the product team's AWS credentials
Because only the product team knows what "normal traffic" looks like for the workload — which fields accept HTML, expected rates, upload endpoints, legitimate bots
Because product teams enjoy writing regular expressions
Because security rules are classified information

questions.question: A rich-text editor in your CMS lets authors paste "<script>" tags intentionally. The OWASP CRS blocks every save with an XSS rule. What is the best fix?
questions.explanation: Surgical scoping is the right answer: exempt the one endpoint where rich HTML is legitimate, keep the rule active everywhere else, and handle sanitisation server-side where context is known.
options: Disable the entire CRS globally
Ask authors to avoid HTML in their articles
Scope the XSS rule to exclude the specific editor endpoint (and sanitize server-side instead)
Lower the paranoia level of every rule to PL1

questions.question: Which statement best captures a WAF's limitations?
questions.explanation: A WAF is not a silver bullet. Pair it with secure coding, SAST/DAST, dependency scanning, bot management and runtime protection for full coverage.
options: A WAF replaces the need for secure coding, SAST and dependency scanning
A WAF stops business-logic abuse and broken authentication out of the box
A WAF is one layer of defence — it does not stop business-logic abuse or attacks that use legitimate API calls in legitimate ways
A WAF makes TLS termination unnecessary
